The hypotheses below rest on the 100 measurements and on how connectivity works in this search space. A recurring pattern: edits matter most when they create or cut a path to the output node, such as adding a missing skip or removing an edge whose loss disconnects the cell.

- **Adding a direct skip (e3) is far more valuable when e3 is 'none'.** It then creates a new residual path. Experiments 13, 14 and 20–22 gain +3 to +45 points, versus +0.2 to +5 when it replaces an existing op (17–19). The exceptions are degenerate all-pool and all-skip cells (15, 16).
- **Edge-removal edits are worst when they disconnect the cell.** Removing e0 with e3 or e1 already 'none' gives drops of up to −78 (30–32). Removing e5 with e4='none' gives drops of up to −76 (64, 65).
- **Skip edits on e4 or e1 help much more when e3='none'.** They supply the missing identity path (82, 88, 90, 94).
- **Turning 'none' into a conv adds a fresh path, so it helps more.** This applies to e5→nor_conv_3x3 when e5 is 'none' (4, 6, 11, 12 vs 79, 80) and to e0→nor_conv_3x3 when e0 is 'none' (75 vs 76–78).
- **Some edits matter more when the target node has only one input.** Adding conv3x3 on e2 helps more when e1='none', because node 2 otherwise depends on e2 alone (52 vs 43). Removing e0 hurts less when e4='none', because node 1 then feeds only e2 (25, 26 vs 23).
- **Pooling on e4 hurts more when e5='none'.** e4 then carries most of the output signal (60 vs 59).
